title: Guided learning paths
intro: A path is a short, ordered route: understand an idea, experience a task, inspect what the result can support, then practise or apply it if it is useful. Every step is optional, untimed, and reversible.
outcomeNotice: Finishing a path means you looked at one idea from several angles. It is not a course grade, a cognitive assessment, or evidence that your ability changed.
boundaryNotice: Educational only. Nothing here diagnoses, treats, or predicts health or everyday performance. Skip or stop at any step; persistent, sudden, or worrying changes deserve qualified care rather than a practice task.

journeys.title: First ten minutes here
journeys.question: What is this place and what can I actually do?
journeys.summary: A short orientation that shows the three moves this space is built around: understand, try, and read the limits. It asks nothing about you and saves nothing.
journeys.outcome: You can name what each area is for, complete one task, and say what its result does not mean.
journeys.boundary: This path is orientation only. It does not measure ability and does not set a goal or target for you.

steps.title: See how the areas connect
steps.purpose: The site is one system: concepts explain, the lab demonstrates, training practises, evidence bounds, and the atlas widens context.
steps.action: Read the five-area explanation, then pick whichever name matches why you came.
steps.takeaway: Each area has one job, and you can move between them without finishing anything.
steps.caution: Labeled links between ideas are relationships, not causes or brain pathways.

steps.title: Do one task once
steps.purpose: A result is easier to interpret when you have produced one yourself.
steps.action: Work through the recall demonstration at your own pace. You decide when to hide the list.
steps.takeaway: One round produces one countable observation about one task.
steps.caution: The count describes this list only. It is not memory capacity, intelligence, or a diagnosis.

steps.title: Read the limits while it is fresh
steps.purpose: Context is most useful before a number starts feeling like a verdict.
steps.action: Open one claim about retrieval practice and inspect its population, design, and stated limitation.
steps.takeaway: You can see which study conditions a statement covers and which it does not.
steps.caution: Review-level findings in classrooms are not proof that this demonstration changes learning.

steps.title: Set the reading conditions you want
steps.purpose: Comfort is a prerequisite for attention; the controls change presentation only.
steps.action: Open Reading options in the header and adjust text size, spacing, contrast, motion, or the reading guide.
steps.linkLabel: Then see how data is handled
steps.takeaway: Preferences stay on this device and never alter what a task reports.
steps.caution: Settings are stored in this browser only; a shared device keeps them until cleared.

steps.title: Choose what to do next
steps.purpose: Leaving with a deliberate choice is the point of an orientation.
steps.action: Decide whether you want a concept, a practice routine, a whole-person area, or nothing further today.
steps.takeaway: You have four legitimate next moves and no obligation to take any of them.
steps.caution: There is no streak, deadline, or penalty for stopping here.

journeys.title: Why do I forget things?
journeys.question: Why do I forget things I knew?
journeys.summary: Forgetfulness is several different things. This path separates keeping, retrieving, and measuring, then lets you experience one small retrieval task and read what it can support.
journeys.outcome: You can explain one reason retrieval can fail and describe your own round without overreading it.
journeys.boundary: Forgetting has many causes, including health conditions this space cannot assess. If forgetting is new, sudden, or interferes with daily safety, that deserves professional evaluation rather than a practice task.

steps.title: Start with what memory means here
steps.purpose: Ordinary language mixes keeping, recalling, and forgetting into one word.
steps.action: Read the memory explanation and its two reviewed claims.
steps.takeaway: A thing can be stored and still fail to come back at a given moment.
steps.caution: The pathway covers a few studied tasks, not your whole life memory.

steps.title: Experience one short recall round
steps.purpose: Retrieval is easier to reason about when you have just attempted it.
steps.action: Study a small list, hide it when ready, and write what comes back.
steps.takeaway: Your result is a count for one list under the conditions you chose.
steps.caution: No timer, no percentile, and no inference about capacity or aging.

steps.title: Meet the neighbouring ideas
steps.purpose: Forgetting is often discussed with working memory and retrieval practice.
steps.action: Follow the related concepts from the memory page and note how each is defined.
steps.takeaway: Related ideas are not interchangeable; each has its own measure.
steps.caution: Relationship labels do not establish mechanism or causation.

steps.title: Check what research actually found
steps.purpose: Retrieval practice is studied with delay tests and classroom materials, not single demos.
steps.action: Read the retrieval evidence section and its limitations.
steps.takeaway: A finding comes with the population and task it was measured on.
steps.caution: Reviewed benefit in a studied context is not a promise for you or for this product.

steps.title: Practise one defined memory task
steps.purpose: Practice should have a target, not a vague 'brain workout'.
steps.action: Choose Sequence Recall or Grid Pattern Recall and read its rules and scoring before starting.
steps.takeaway: Improvement, if any, is described for that task and item set.
steps.caution: Task improvement is not general memory improvement or transfer to daily life.

steps.title: Take one idea off the screen
steps.purpose: The useful test is whether an idea changes how you study tomorrow.
steps.action: Use the memory and learning pathway's starter steps for one real item you need to keep.
steps.linkLabel: Open the memory and learning pathway
steps.takeaway: You leave with a small, optional action rather than a score to defend.
steps.caution: Adapt or skip any step; the pathway is an educational suggestion, not a prescription.

journeys.title: Why does my focus come and go?
journeys.question: Why can't I stay focused?
journeys.summary: Focus is described here as a task-level behaviour rather than a personality trait. The path pairs an attention explanation with a counting task and an explicit note on what a score cannot say.
journeys.outcome: You can describe one attention task, its result, and at least two reasons a single round is weak evidence.
journeys.boundary: Persistent attention difficulties have many causes, including conditions this space does not assess. Only a qualified professional can evaluate them.

steps.title: Read what attention refers to here
steps.purpose: 'Focus' is used for selection, sustained effort, and multitasking alike.
steps.action: Open the attention concept and note which use each claim addresses.
steps.takeaway: The word covers several measurable things; the task names which one.
steps.caution: A task definition is not a clinical definition.

steps.title: Try a scanning task with no countdown
steps.purpose: A small search task makes selection concrete without speed pressure.
steps.action: Count the target letters in a grid at your own pace.
steps.takeaway: Accuracy here belongs to these five static grids.
steps.caution: It does not measure everyday attention, ADHD, or visual health.

steps.title: See how task context changes results
steps.purpose: Attention findings depend heavily on the task and setting used.
steps.action: Read the attention and task-context evidence with its limitations.
steps.takeaway: You can tell a task-level observation from a general claim.
steps.caution: Reviewed associations are not explanations of your day.

steps.title: Adjust one condition, not your character
steps.purpose: Small environment and sequencing changes are testable; self-criticism is not.
steps.action: Work through the attention and executive-skills pathway's starter.
steps.takeaway: You have one concrete change to try on your own terms.
steps.caution: Nothing here is a productivity system or treatment.

steps.title: Notice what the task could not tell you
steps.purpose: Naming missing context prevents over-interpretation.
steps.action: Write down what you would need to know before trusting this round as a pattern.
steps.takeaway: A pattern needs repeated, comparable rounds and stated conditions.
steps.caution: Saved sessions are only the ones you chose to keep on this device.

journeys.title: How should I actually study?
journeys.question: How do I learn material so it stays?
journeys.summary: A learning-science route through retrieval practice, spacing, and the difference between feeling familiar and being able to recall. It links reviewed sources to a demonstration you can run in minutes.
journeys.outcome: You can describe one high-utility technique, one honest limit of the evidence, and one way to apply it to your own material.
journeys.boundary: Study guidance is general. Courses, materials, age, disability, and language differ; adapt with your instructor, tutor, or clinician where accommodations matter.

steps.title: Learn what retrieval practice is
steps.purpose: Trying to recall is different from re-reading, and the difference is the whole idea.
steps.action: Read the retrieval-practice pathway and its claims.
steps.takeaway: Recall attempts can be part of learning, not just proof of it.
steps.caution: The reviewed effect varies with material, delay, and test conditions.

steps.title: Run one recall round yourself
steps.purpose: Feeling fluent and being able to recall can diverge; a short round makes that noticeable.
steps.action: Complete the word-recall demonstration and read its result wording carefully.
steps.takeaway: You have one personal data point about one list.
steps.caution: No delayed test means no claim about long-term retention.

steps.title: Separate performance from learning
steps.purpose: What you can do right after practice and what survives a week are different measures.
steps.action: Read the learning pathway and notice where delay appears in the study designs.
steps.takeaway: A technique claim needs a follow-up test to be about learning.
steps.caution: This product does not administer delayed tests.

steps.title: Check which techniques were rated highly
steps.purpose: Common study habits are not equally supported.
steps.action: Read the practice-techniques claim with its source scope and limitations.
steps.takeaway: You can see a review's rating and its boundaries together.
steps.caution: A review-level rating is not guaranteed for every learner or subject.

steps.title: Build the technique into one real session
steps.purpose: The transfer question is whether it survives contact with your actual material.
steps.action: Follow the memory and learning pathway's starter with something you genuinely need to know.
steps.takeaway: One concrete session plan you can adjust or abandon.
steps.caution: No dose, deadline, or promised grade improvement is implied.

journeys.title: How do I reason more carefully?
journeys.question: Am I reasoning well or just feeling sure?
journeys.audience: people who want a slower thinking habit
journeys.summary: A short route through inference from stated premises, pattern prediction, and metacognitive checking. It keeps confidence and accuracy as separate observations.
journeys.outcome: You can name the difference between a conclusion that follows from the premises and one that merely feels right.
journeys.boundary: These tasks practise specific item sets. They do not measure reasoning ability, IQ, or judgment in real situations where information is incomplete and stakes matter.

steps.title: Answer from stated premises only
steps.purpose: The fastest way to feel the premise/conclusion gap is to be held to it.
steps.action: Open Logic Lab, read its rules, and complete one five-item session.
steps.takeaway: Some conclusions follow, and some are merely possible.
steps.caution: Correct answers here do not indicate general reasoning skill.

steps.title: Predict the next item in a pattern
steps.purpose: Pattern tasks show how much a rule is underdetermined by a few examples.
steps.action: Try Pattern Predictor and read each explanation, right or wrong.
steps.takeaway: Several rules can fit the same first few items.
steps.caution: Feedback is item-specific, not a reasoning profile.

steps.title: Read why a task score is bounded
steps.purpose: The boundary is the most useful part of the result.
steps.action: Open the activity-boundary section of the evidence page.
steps.takeaway: Item set, difficulty, and practice effects are not controlled across sessions.
steps.caution: Nothing here is a validated assessment or a diagnosis.

steps.title: Add a confidence check to one decision
steps.purpose: Metacognition is checking your own evidence, not thinking harder.
steps.action: Use the metacognition pathway's starter on a real choice you are facing today.
steps.takeaway: One question you can ask yourself before committing.
steps.caution: Reflection is not a mood, personality, or mental-health assessment.

journeys.title: Does sleep really change thinking?
journeys.question: How much does sleep matter for my mind?
journeys.audience: anyone tempted to trade sleep for study or work
journeys.summary: Sleep is presented as interacting context, not a score to optimise. The path reads population guidance, uses a local-only window sketch, and stops well short of sleep advice.
journeys.outcome: You can describe one studied link between sleep and memory and state why this page cannot tell you your personal sleep need.
journeys.boundary: Not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment, and not a sleep assessment. Concerns such as snoring, sudden sleepiness, or persistent insomnia need qualified care; the planner records nothing about you.

steps.title: Read the reviewed sleep and memory statements
steps.purpose: Claims about sleep and memory are specific about population, design, and outcome.
steps.action: Open the sleep pathway and its three claims with their limitations.
steps.takeaway: Research describes group-level findings under named conditions.
steps.caution: No individual can be scored from this page.

steps.title: Sketch an opportunity window
steps.purpose: Arithmetic makes the difference between time in bed and possible sleep concrete.
steps.action: Enter a wake time and a window you choose. Nothing is saved or sent.
steps.takeaway: A short window cannot contain a longer amount of actual sleep.
steps.caution: This is clock arithmetic, not sleep quality, need, or health.

steps.title: See the guidance as guidance
steps.purpose: Population recommendations vary by age and circumstance and are not prescriptions.
steps.action: Read the sleep evidence with its stated scope and limits.
steps.takeaway: You can tell a guideline from a personal target.
steps.caution: Consensus guidance does not diagnose or predict your cognition.

steps.title: Handle recovery as a context, not a scoreboard
steps.purpose: Tracking can help some people and pressure others; the atlas keeps it optional and unmeasured.
steps.action: Read the sleep and recovery pathway, its starter, and its care boundary.
steps.linkLabel: Open the sleep and recovery pathway
steps.takeaway: One adaptable, low-burden idea to consider off-screen.
steps.caution: No sleep score, streak, or wake-alarm behaviour is offered here.
